editorial_contributions.text:
A periodic monohedral tiling of the plane may be considered as a map to be colored under the usual rule that adjacent tiles get different colors; the chromatic number \(\chi\) is 2,3. or 4. For some tilings, there is a unique coloring (up to color permutation) with \(\chi\) colors (for \(N>\chi\), \(N\)-colorings are never unique.) Such a unique coloring must be periodic.

If a tiling allows more than one \(N\)-coloring, it is possible to reduce the choice with a \textit{seed}, a finite set of tiles whose colors are specified. A seed is called \textit{perfect} if it is consistent with a unique \(N\)-coloring: the author shows that the coloring forced by a perfect seed may be aperiodic, and studies this phenomenon. One interesting result: for the Cairo tiling and \(N=4\), there are, up to equivalence, exactly two full colorings that are forced by finite seeds, both aperiodic.

The author also considers \textit{decent} seeds, those that are consistent with a finite set of global colorings, and exhibits a 2-tile seed for the Cairo tiling that allows exactly 36 4-colorings.
